title: 75 Divorced People Share The One Thing They Wish Someone Had Told Them Before The Wedding
text: 75 Divorced People Share The One Thing They Wish Someone Had Told Them Before The Wedding Nobody walks down the aisle thinking they will end up as a cautionary tale. But the people in this thread learned everything about marriage the hard way and came back to share it for free. The least you can do is read it before you book the venue. . You walk down the aisle thinking about the flowers, the speech, and whether the caterer has sorted the vegetarian option. Divorce is never part of the plan, which is exactly why people who have been through it have so much to say about\"the plan. \"what they wished they had known before the wedding, and the thread is one of the more useful documents on the internet for anyone who is currently engaged, recently married, or simply curious about what people on the other side learned the hard way. Sadly, someone had to go through it; the least we can do is listen and learn. My friend going through a divorce admitted she wanted the wedding, not the marriage.She had pics published in magazines, went over the top wherever she could. She needed a reason to celebrate herself and feel special. PLEASE know you do not have to have a wedding to justify a white tie soirée. Love is only a part of it.If you're not compatible in many other ways, you're destined for failure. Sure: money, religion, politics, having kids. But also other things. If one of you is doing 95% of the cooking and cleaning, that person is going to be tired and cranky all the time and there are going to be arguments and resentment.I knew she was volatile, but it wasn't really directed at people. Her antics were funny and seemed mostly performative. It wasn't until we had a child that I really understood just how disturbed she was. Seeing her direct her rage at our infant son isn't something I'll ever forget.One of the most consistent themes across the thread is not infidelity or incompatibility as you'd expect. It is the things people noticed before the wedding and talked themselves out of. Research from thefound that the information needed to predict whether a relationship will succeed is almost always available before marriage, and that the couples who divorce report, in retrospect, having had doubts they dismissed as nerves.Dr. John Gottman has studied couples for over four decades and can predict divorce with 94% accuracy from a single conversation.\"People often know something is wrong long before they are willing to admit it,\" he said. So regardless of whether the venue was already booked, the red flags were there, and your gut was screaming at you. That I would always come in third place when it came to his time and attention. His job was first, then his children , then me\/our marriage.For ten years. Their credit score, we went to apply for a car loan shortly after and mine was 800+ theirs was like 250. I immediately knew they couldn't be trusted with finances. They said I was being controlling while they hid payday loans.Luckily I was young and got out quickly. I told my current GF even if we get married our bank accounts will be separate and I would get a prenup. we can have a joint account to pay shared bills. That she may or may not have truly been in love with me when she said that she wanted to get married and she did so thinking that I would be the one to “save” her from herself.She ended up being disappointed over the years until she emotionally checked out and allowed another dude to come between us and our marriage. She then broke up with me, blindsided and traumatised our kids. Destroying whatever we were trying to build in the first place. That marriage and kids with someone doesn’t make them entitled to your life.I treat her as if she’s a distant relative these days. I’m a single parent and she hardly sees the children. They too treat her like she’s a passerby to our lives. No longer integral or relevant to our present and future lives., the four communication patterns that predict the end of a relationship reliably. Number one is criticism, landing blows on the partner's personality rather than their behavior.Next is contempt, which includes eye-rolling, sarcasm, and treating a partner as inferior. Defensiveness is next: refusing to accept any responsibility. And stonewalling, the complete emotional shutdown during conflict. Of the four, contempt is the single most reliable predictor of divorce, which means the partner who rolls their eyes during an argument is sending a more significant signal than most people register at the time.That may sound stupid, but the pressure to get married was so incredibly high, there was no way I could see for me to not go through with it. That divorce can, indeed, happen to you, no matter your best intentions going in. And it's likely not going to be easy and clean.found that finances are the leading cause of stress in relationships, cited by 35% of respondents, ahead of every other source of conflict.But the problem isn't always just about how MUCH money there is. It is the difference in values around money, one person spending freely while the other saves anxiously, or one person hiding purchases while the other demands financial transparency. Couples who have explicit conversations about money before marriage, about debt, spending habits, financial goals, and who pays for what, have measurably lower divorce rates than those who assume they will figure it out as they go.Spoiler: They do not figure it out as they go. I wish we talked about the future more because I knew I couldn't have children and told my ex-husband as such when we started dating at 18 and reiterated it again when we got married at 25... He said he didn't care. That he loved me.Flashforward 10 years, he leaves me in May and divorces me in July saying that I pulled one over on him. I didn't understand that some people literally don't have the ability to think from another person's perspective. I thought I could just keep explaining and something would click for my husband and he would treat me better.I think we all have a lot of implicit asumptions about what married life actually looks like and how everything works, and it's not until after we are married that we realise that we were not agreeing to the same things. Some of it is big things, like whether getting married automatically means having children or combining finances.are filed by women, climbing to 90% among college-educated women.Research from the American Sociological Association found that women in heterosexual marriages report lower relationship quality on average than their husbands, are more likely to identify problems in the relationship, and are more likely to initiate the conversation about those problems. The marriages that end are disproportionately the ones where those conversations were not received well.The women in this thread who say they wish they had paid attention to how their partner handled being told something difficult are pointing at the same data from a personal angle. That my fear was not unfounded. His resistance and struggles to discuss his difficult feelings would indeed be our demise. When he blindsided me with divorce he did it crying and telling me he wished he had listened to me but now it was too late.While many of these comments are from victims of violence and I don't intend to downplay that, the number of people who blame their ex for all of their problems and don't do any self reflection on how they wish they could have had a wiser perspective is startlingly high. As for me... I wish that I had known just how much my trauma had affected me, and that faith and prayer are not enough.In fact, I wish I had known that prayer, really, mostly just affirms one's own gut feelings and biases. If I had had half the growth I have had since then, I could have reduced the pain we put each other through immensely, or even just not gotten married in the first place.The average marriage that ends in divorce lasts eight years, which means the problems visible in retrospect were present and compounding for the better part of a decade. The\"\" has a basis in research, with studies showing a dip in marital satisfaction around years five to seven as the neurochemical effects of early romantic love stabilize and the relationship settles into its actual daily shape.The person you marry in the honeymoon period is not the person you will be having a disagreement with about the dishwasher in year six. Meeting that person before the wedding would have been useful, so listen when people warn you about this.found that couples who participate in premarital education programs have a 30% lower divorce rate than those who do not, and report higher levels of communication quality and relationship satisfaction in the years that follow.Despite this, only around 30% of couples who get married in the US attend any form of premarital counseling, largely because it carries the implication that something is already wrong. The reframe that researchers suggest is straightforward: you would not buy a house without an inspection. The inspection is not an insult to the house. - marrying for the persons potential in the future is the most risky thing you can do.Bet on yourself than your to be spouse- You can divorce early if you realize that the person is not going to change- Married life should make you happy overall . it shouldn’t make you more depressed and anxious. That though we will always be who we were when we committed ourselves to each other with tears in our eyes, our idea of life changes as we mature.They will always need the safety of predictability and the comfort of knowing whats next in life. It doesn’t mean that we didn’t absolutely love the things out of each other and want to spend the rest of our lives together. We meant it, but as we grew, we realized that sometimes compromising ourselves to appease the one we love, breeds contempt. She went on crazy adventures with me, and I settled down with her.We tried to be what the other wanted because we loved being with each other and deserved to be with the person they wanted. After twenty something years it was apparent that we would be living a life of lukewarm satisfaction until she passes peacefully in her sleep and I drown trying to swim out to where I can barely see land, just to find out if I can make it back.Marriage is a story, its safety and adventure into the unknown of what makes life wonderful. It teaches us about trust, and compromise. It teaches us how to put someone before our selves. If you love this person, nothing will top the regret you will hold if you don’t at least give it a try.Even the heartbreak of realizing it doesn’t work doesn’t compare to the heartbreak of never giving all of yourself to the one you love.
